lead: Hardware-software co-design is the practice of deciding early which parts of an embedded system run as custom hardware and which run as software on a processor. The decision is made together, not one side after the other, because speed, power, chip area, flexibility and time-to-market all pull in different directions. A camera pipeline, a car braking controller and a UPI payment terminal all face the same choice: put a function in a fast fixed circuit or in a programmable CPU. Co-design makes that split visible before detailed design starts.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.4 for the design stages and Unit 1 for processor choices.

blocks.text: Co-design starts with a specification that states what the system must do, at what rate, with what latency and within what power budget. The specification is executable: a model produces test data that both hardware and software teams can use. Partitioning follows. Each function is placed in custom hardware, in software on a processor, or in a mix. The split is recorded with reasons, because late changes cost money and time. Interface design comes next: data width, handshake signals, memory map, interrupt lines and driver boundary.

items: Write an executable specification with rate, latency and power targets.
Partition functions into hardware and software; record why for each function.
Define the interface contract: data width, handshake, memory map and interrupts.
Design hardware by synthesis or FPGA mapping; compile software with a cross-toolchain in parallel.
Co-simulate both sides with shared test vectors.
Integrate on the target board and test the complete system.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this HW/SW co-design. Five axes decide the split: speed, power, area, flexibility and time-to-market.

items: Speed: custom hardware can run many operations in parallel; software runs one instruction stream on a CPU.
Power: a fixed datapath often uses less energy per operation than fetch-and-execute software, but only if it stays busy.
Area: hardware consumes chip area or FPGA logic; software reuses one processor for many functions.
Flexibility: software can be patched after shipping; fixed hardware cannot, unless it is reconfigurable.
Time-to-market: hardware design, verification and mask costs add months; software changes are cheaper.

blocks.text: A hardware accelerator is a fixed datapath that replaces a hot loop. An application-specific instruction set processor (ASIP) is a CPU with custom instructions for one domain. A reusable block licensed from a vendor or taken from a library is an IP core. Platform-based design starts from a validated processor, bus and memory base, then adds blocks. These choices reduce risk, but they also add interface cost. A fast accelerator still needs a FIFO, DMA or bus transfer, a driver and verification. Formal partitioning algorithms exist, but only a few universities teach them; most teams use profiling plus experience. FPGA details appear in Chapter 6.7, and power techniques in Chapter 6.9.

The interface contract is the boundary between the two designs. It fixes data width, clock domain, transfer rate, handshake protocol, register map and interrupt behaviour. A wrong width or a missing ready signal can make a correct accelerator useless. On-chip buses such as those in Unit 4 carry the data; the driver in software must match the hardware registers exactly.

Co-simulation runs the hardware model and the compiled software model together. Shared test vectors check that both sides agree on timing and data. Integration then follows a fixed order: boot the processor, test the bus, test each register, run a small transfer, then run the full workload. This order finds interface faults before they hide inside application code.

figure.caption: The specification is split into hardware and software, then co-simulated and integrated. Notice that the partition is one early step, not a late fix.

spec.title: Co-design split
spec.aria: A specification is partitioned into hardware and software designs, which are co-simulated and then integrated into one system.

examples.question: A 640×480 camera runs at 30 frames/s. Each pixel needs 20 operations. A 200 MIPS CPU runs the filter in software. Find the operation rate and the CPU load. If an FPGA accelerator does 1 operation per cycle at 100 MHz, how many parallel units are needed? Treat one operation as one instruction for this estimate.
steps: One FPGA unit capacity = 1 operation/cycle × 100,000,000 cycles/s = 100,000,000 operations/s = 100 Mops/s.
examples.answer: The filter needs 184,320,000 operations/s, which is 92.16% CPU load; two 100 Mops/s FPGA units are needed.
examples.check:
import math
w=640
h=480
fps=30
ops_per_pixel=20
ops_per_s=w*h*ops_per_pixel*fps
cpu_mips=200
cpu_ops_per_s=cpu_mips*1000000
load_percent=ops_per_s/cpu_ops_per_s*100
freq_mhz=100
ops_per_cycle=1
cap_ops_per_s=freq_mhz*1000000*ops_per_cycle
units=math.ceil(ops_per_s/cap_ops_per_s)
print(ops_per_s)
print(round(load_percent,2))
print(int(cap_ops_per_s/1000000))
print(units)

traps: Choosing hardware only for speed while ignoring interface cost, verification effort and loss of flexibility.
Treating MIPS as operations per second without checking the instruction mix; one operation may need several instructions.
Forgetting to round up when buying parallel accelerator units; 1.84 units means 2 units.
Assuming co-design means hardware first and software later; the split must be decided before both detailed designs.
Ignoring data-rate multiplication: resolution and frame rate both raise the operation rate.

quiz.a: It is the early, joint decision of which system functions run in custom hardware and which run in software, with interface and verification planned together.

quiz.q: Name four stages of the co-design flow.
quiz.a: Specification, partitioning, interface design, hardware and software design, co-simulation, integration. Any four are correct.
Late changes force redesign of both hardware and software. Early partitioning fixes interfaces, budgets verification effort and protects time-to-market.

quiz.q: A 320×240 camera runs at 25 frames/s. Each pixel needs 10 operations. A 50 MIPS CPU runs the filter. Find the operation rate and CPU load.
For the camera in the previous question, an FPGA unit does 1 operation per cycle at 50 MHz. How many units are needed?
quiz.a: One unit capacity = 50,000,000 operations/s = 50 Mops/s. Units = ceil(19,200,000 ÷ 50,000,000) = ceil(0.384) = 1 unit.

quiz.q: In a camera system, which function would you put in hardware and which in software? Justify briefly.
quiz.a: Put the per-pixel filter in hardware because it repeats millions of times per second and benefits from parallelism. Keep auto-exposure control in software because it changes rarely, needs tuning and benefits from flexibility.

quiz.q: A hardware accelerator is faster than software. Give two reasons it may still be the wrong choice.
quiz.a: It adds interface, driver and verification cost. It also removes flexibility, so a late algorithm change becomes a hardware redesign.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses virtual platforms to run software before chips exist, and high-level synthesis to turn C models into hardware. RISC-V custom instructions are a current route to ASIPs. Search for electronic system-level design, platform-based design, high-level synthesis and virtual prototypes.
